concepts.title: Queues, at-least-once delivery and event-driven systems

misconceptions.description: All 4xx statuses are thought to be permanent client errors that never succeed on retry, though some, such as 429 or 408, are routinely retried. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: Every 4xx error is permanent

misconceptions.description: A retry is thought to be protected by having some key, even when every attempt uses a different one. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: Any idempotency key makes a retry safe

misconceptions.description: At-least-once delivery is thought to deliver every message two times. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: At-least-once means twice

misconceptions.description: A loop that records a key and then breaks is thought to break first. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: The loop stops before the last attempt is recorded

misconceptions.description: The compensations of a saga are thought to run in the order the steps were done. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: Compensations run oldest first

misconceptions.description: A message delivered twice is thought to be a defect of the queue, though redelivery is how at-least-once avoids loss. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: A duplicate delivery is a queue bug

misconceptions.description: The step that failed is thought to be undone as well, though it did not finish. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: The failed step is compensated

misconceptions.description: Duplicate charges are thought to show that the service does not deduplicate, although the client may have defeated a working key check. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: Duplicate charges mean the bank has no protection

misconceptions.description: After an error that should not be retried, the function is thought to run on to its final return. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: A non-retryable error does not stop the retry function

misconceptions.description: A queue is thought to deliver each message exactly once, even when a consumer dies before acknowledging. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: The queue delivers exactly once

misconceptions.description: An unacknowledged message is thought to be delivered again behind the later messages, though the queue keeps it at the front. Distinct from prod.broker-sorts-by-failure-count and the returned-message order of the redelivery question. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: An unacknowledged message is redelivered last

misconceptions.description: All errors, including permanent client errors, are thought to be worth retrying. Distinct from prod.retry-covers-all-failures: this concerns which statuses are retried, that one concerns which exception types the loop catches. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: Every error is retried

misconceptions.description: The undo of a saga is thought to be a transactional rollback instead of explicit compensating steps. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: Compensation is a database rollback

misconceptions.description: The effects of finished steps are thought to be undone without any compensating action. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: A saga rolls back by itself

misconceptions.description: A 5xx status such as 503 is thought not to be retried, so the first failure ends the loop. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: A server error is not retried

misconceptions.description: A request that the client gave up on is thought never to have been processed by the service. Distinct from prod.timeout-cancels-server-work: here the request is thought never to have been processed; there it was processed and then undone. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: A timed-out request never reached the service

misconceptions.description: The client giving up is thought to cancel or undo the request at the service, so only the successful attempt has any effect. Distinct from prod.timed-out-request-never-processed: here the request is thought to have been processed and then undone, and the processed count still includes it. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: A client timeout cancels the work at the service

misconceptions.description: A timeout is thought to be checked only once the call has returned, so the client waits out the full latency before treating it as timed out. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: A timeout fires after the call has finished

misconceptions.description: After a timeout, the late service value is thought to be returned to the caller as a result, instead of an exception being raised. Editorial hypothesis.
misconceptions.title: A timed-out call still returns its late value
